elements.quote: Cite this article as: ceravolo MG, andrenelli E, arienti c, côté p, de sire a, iannicelli V, et al .; the international Multiprofessional steering committee of cochrane rehabilitation rEh-coVEr action. rehabilitation and coVid-19: rapid living systematic review by cochrane rehabilitation field - third edition.
elements.reason: The abstract citation block explicitly identifies the report as a 'rapid living systematic review'.

elements.quote: introduction: this paper updates and summarizes the current evidence informing rehabilitation of patients with coVid-19 and/or describing the consequences of the disease and its treatment.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states the objective to update and summarize evidence on rehabilitation and consequences of COVID-19.

elements.quote: EVidEncE acQuisition: studies published from May 1 st to June 30 th , 2021 were selected, excluding descriptive studies and expert opinions.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the inclusion timeframe and exclusion criteria (descriptive studies and expert opinions).
The abstract mentions the publication date range but does not identify the specific information sources or databases used to search for studies.

elements.quote: from this edition, we improved the quality assessment using the Joanna briggs institute checklists for observational studies and the cochrane risk of bias tool for randomized-controlled clinical trials (rcts).
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the tools used for risk of bias assessment (JBI checklists and Cochrane RoB tool).

elements.quote: EVIDENCE SYNTHESIS: Twenty-five, out of 3699 papers, were included. They were three RCTs, 13 cross-sectional studies and nine cohort studies.
elements.reason: The abstract describes the categorization of studies but does not explicitly name the synthesis method (e.g., narrative synthesis) used to combine results.

elements.quote: Twenty-five, out of 3699 papers, were included... all study participants were coVid survivors and 48% of studies collected information on participants 6 months or longer after coVid-19 onset.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (25) and participant characteristics, but does not provide the total number of participants across studies.

elements.quote: conclusions: Most studies in this updated review targeted the prevalence of limitations of functioning of rehabilitation interest in coVID-19 survivors.
elements.reason: The abstract summarizes the nature of the results qualitatively but does not present specific quantitative results for the main outcomes (e.g., prevalence rates).

elements.quote: This third edition still provides a narrative synthesis of findings, as a meta-analysis is not applicable due to the high heterogeneity of the studies.
elements.reason: A meta-analysis was not conducted, so this conditional element does not apply.
The abstract does not report comparisons between groups with effect directions, as the review focuses on prevalence and natural history without meta-analysis.

elements.quote: the most frequent risks of bias for rcts concerned weaknesses in allocation concealment, blinding of therapists, and lack of intention-to-treat analysis. Most analytical studies failed to identify or deal with confounders...
elements.reason: The abstract summarizes important limitations regarding risk of bias and methodological quality.

elements.quote: There is a need for good quality intervention efficacy and effectiveness studies to complement the rapidly expanding evidence from observational studies.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation and implication regarding the need for future high-quality studies.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.
The abstract does not provide the register name and registration number (PROSPERO) for the review protocol.

elements.quote: A high proportion of SARS-CoV-2 patients survive infection but the prevalence of chronic sequelae and resulting disability is increasing. These survivors need clinical management and rehabilitation to facilitate good health outcomes.
elements.reason: The rationale section describes the current state of knowledge (high proportion of survivors with chronic sequelae) and uncertainties (need for clinical management and rehabilitation).

elements.quote: The best available research evidence is required to inform management and rehabilitation decisions, interventions, and health systems for COVID-19 survivors with adverse clinical sequelae. Further evidence is warranted to estimate the resources needed to plan for setting appropriate and adequately delivered post-acute and long-term rehabilitation services.
elements.reason: The rationale section explains the importance and need for the review by stating that best available evidence is required to inform decisions and that further evidence is warranted to estimate resources.

elements.quote: This rapid living systematic review on rehabilitation and COVID-19 was initiated in April 2020 as a component of the Cochrane Rehabilitation REH-COVER action. 3 Since its inception, it has been updated monthly, with the most recent update leading to a total of 319 papers up to April 30 th , 2021.
elements.reason: The rationale section identifies the previous review (initiated in April 2020, updated monthly) and explains the need for the current review (recent increase in analytical studies encouraged advancing methodology).
The rationale section does not describe the proposed mechanism of action of the rehabilitation interventions, which is required for reviews of intervention effects.
The rationale section does not mention considering a logic model to show hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes, which is required for complex interventions.

elements.quote: introduction: this paper updates and summarizes the current evidence informing rehabilitation of patients with coVid-19 and/or describing the consequences of the disease and its treatment.
elements.reason: The objective is explicitly stated in the abstract/introduction section, defining the scope as updating and summarizing evidence on rehabilitation and consequences of COVID-19.
